title: JEZEBEL WAS THROWN FROM A WINDOW. WHEN THEY CAME BACK FOR HER BODY, THE DOGS HAD LEFT ALMOST NOTHING.
paragraphs: JEZEBEL WAS THROWN FROM A WINDOW. WHEN THEY CAME BACK FOR HER BODY, THE DOGS HAD LEFT ALMOST NOTHING.

She wore a crown, commanded a kingdom, and believed she could silence the voice of God. But her terrifying ending reveals something far more important than how a wicked queen died: what happens when a human heart keeps rejecting the mercy of God—and why Jesus Christ is still calling sinners to repentance before it is too late.
“And they went to bury her: but they found no more of her than the skull, and the feet, and the palms of her hands.” — 2 Kings 9:35 (KJV)
There is something deeply unsettling about a woman who once had everything being reduced to almost nothing.
Not because she was poor.
Not because she was forgotten.
But because she had spent years convincing herself that no one could touch her.
She had power. She had influence. She had servants who obeyed her commands. She had a king beside her and an entire nation trembling under the shadow of her decisions.
And then came the day when even her royal name could not protect her.
The Bible tells us that when men returned to bury Jezebel, they could not find her body intact.
Only her skull.
Her feet.
And the palms of her hands.
The rest had been consumed by dogs.
But before you picture that horrifying scene and quickly conclude, “She deserved it,” there is something you need to understand.
The most frightening thing about Jezebel's story is not what happened to her body. It is what had already happened to her heart.
And if we are willing to be honest, her story may expose something in us that we would rather leave untouched.
Because Jezebel did not become the woman we remember in a single day.
Her destruction had a history.
And so does every heart that slowly learns to live without repentance.

Jezebel was the daughter of Ethbaal, king of the Sidonians, and the wife of Ahab, king of Israel (1 Kings 16:31). Her arrival in Israel was more than a royal marriage. Scripture records that Ahab served Baal and worshiped him, building an altar for Baal in Samaria.
The worship of the living God was being displaced by idolatry.
And Jezebel was no passive observer.

She actively supported the prophets of Baal and Asherah, while the prophets of the LORD faced persecution. First Kings 18:4 records that Jezebel had cut off the prophets of the LORD, forcing Obadiah to hide one hundred of them in caves.
Think about that.
People were hiding because they refused to abandon the God of Israel.
Faithfulness had become dangerous.
And the woman sitting in the palace was helping make it so.
But perhaps one of the clearest windows into Jezebel's character appears in a story that begins with something surprisingly ordinary.
A vineyard.
A man named Naboth owned a vineyard near Ahab's palace. The king wanted it for himself. He offered Naboth money or another vineyard in exchange.
Naboth refused.
Not because he wanted to insult the king, but because the land was his ancestral inheritance, and he understood that inheritance in light of God's covenant with Israel.
“The LORD forbid it me, that I should give the inheritance of my fathers unto thee.” (1 Kings 21:3, KJV)
Ahab returned home resentful, lay on his bed, turned away, and refused to eat.
When Jezebel discovered why he was upset, she took matters into her own hands.
She wrote letters in Ahab's name, sealed them with his seal, and arranged for false witnesses to accuse Naboth of blaspheming God and the king.
Naboth was taken outside the city and stoned to death.
An innocent man lost his life because someone powerful wanted what belonged to him.
And when Jezebel heard that Naboth was dead, she told Ahab to take possession of the vineyard.
Read that slowly.
A man's life had been destroyed.
His inheritance had been stolen.
His name had been disgraced through lies.
And the palace carried on.
That is what unrepentant sin can do to the human heart.
It can make another person's suffering seem like a small price to pay for getting what we want.
Perhaps you have never worn a crown or ordered someone's death.
But have you ever justified hurting someone because you felt entitled to something?
Have you ever twisted the truth to protect your reputation?
Have you ever watched another person suffer because of your choices, yet convinced yourself that you were the one who had been wronged?
This is where the story becomes uncomfortable.
Because Scripture was not written merely to give us villains to despise.
It also exposes the darkness that human beings are capable of when desire becomes an idol and conscience is repeatedly ignored.
Jeremiah 17:9 warns that the heart is deceitful above all things and desperately wicked.
And Romans 3:23 declares:
“For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God.” (KJV)
Not just Jezebel.
Not just Ahab.
All.
Including the person writing these words.
Including the person reading them.
But there is something remarkable in the account of Naboth.
God saw what happened.
The lies did not fool Him.
The royal seal did not intimidate Him.
The grave did not silence the testimony of innocent blood.
Through the prophet Elijah, the LORD confronted Ahab and announced judgment upon his house. The prophecy also declared that dogs would eat Jezebel by the wall of Jezreel (1 Kings 21:23).
Yet even in that dark chapter, we encounter something astonishing.
When Ahab heard God's judgment, he humbled himself, tore his clothes, wore sackcloth, and fasted.
And God took notice.
In 1 Kings 21:29, the LORD told Elijah that because Ahab had humbled himself, the announced disaster upon his house would not come during his own days.
Ahab's response did not erase his crimes or cancel every consequence. But it revealed something essential about God's character.
God does not delight in human wickedness, and He does not overlook genuine humility.
Even a deeply corrupt king was not beyond being confronted by the word of God.
And that makes Jezebel's story even more sobering.
Because the warning had been spoken.
The truth had been made known.
The kingdom had witnessed God's power.
But the biblical narrative records no comparable repentance from Jezebel.
Years passed.
Ahab died.
The consequences of the royal house's wickedness continued to unfold.
And eventually a man named Jehu came riding toward Jezreel.

Second Kings 9 describes Jehu's anointing and his violent campaign against Ahab's dynasty. The chapter presents his actions in the context of the announced judgment upon that house, though the broader biblical account does not give Jehu unlimited moral approval for everything he would do.
When Jezebel heard that Jehu had come, she did something extraordinary.
She painted her eyes.
She arranged her hair.
And she looked out through a window.
Second Kings 9:30 records those details.

We should not pretend to know every thought in her mind. Scripture does not explicitly tell us whether she was trying to intimidate Jehu, preserve her royal dignity, or confront him through a calculated display of authority.
But it tells us what she said.
“Had Zimri peace, who slew his master?” (2 Kings 9:31, KJV)
Zimri was a previous assassin who had seized Israel's throne and whose reign ended after only seven days. Jezebel's words invoked that bloody precedent as Jehu approached.
Even now, with judgment at her door, she spoke from the window of the palace.
Jehu looked up and asked who was on his side.
Two or three eunuchs looked out.
Jehu commanded them to throw her down.
And they did.
Her blood struck the wall and the horses, and Jehu trampled her underfoot.
It is a brutal scene.
Scripture does not invite us to enjoy the suffering. It records the severity of the event and the fulfillment of the prophetic warning.
Afterward, Jehu went inside, ate, and drank.
Then he gave an order to bury Jezebel, saying she was a king's daughter.
But by the time the men returned to collect her body, almost nothing remained.
The skull.
The feet.
The palms of her hands.
The Hebrew of 2 Kings 9:35 reads:
וַיֵּלְכוּ לְקָבְרָהּ וְלֹא־מָצְאוּ בָהּ כִּי אִם־הַגֻּלְגֹּלֶת וְהָרַגְלַיִם וְכַפּוֹת הַיָּדָיִם
Vayyelekhū leqovrāh, velo-matse'ū vāh kī 'im-haggulgōlet vehāraglayim vekhappōt hayyādayim.
In context, the Hebrew says that they went to bury her but found nothing of her except the skull, the feet, and the palms of the hands.
The word גֻּלְגֹּלֶת (gulgōlet) means “skull.”
The word רַגְלַיִם (raglayim) refers to “feet.”
And כַּפּוֹת הַיָּדַיִם (kappōt hayyādayim) refers to the palms of the hands.
These are not mystical symbols secretly encoded in the passage.
They are the physical remains the biblical narrator identifies.
And the terrible incompleteness of those remains underscores the disgrace of Jezebel's death and the fulfillment of God's announced judgment.
When Jehu heard what had happened, he recognized the fulfillment of the word spoken through Elijah.

Second Kings 9:36–37 connects the dogs consuming Jezebel with the prophecy that her remains would become like dung upon the field, so that no one could identify her burial place and say, “This is Jezebel.”
The woman whose influence had once dominated a royal court was denied even the lasting honor of a recognizable grave.
And yet the deeper message is not that every wicked person will die in such a manner.
Scripture does not teach that.
Nor does it teach that every tragedy is God's direct punishment for a particular sin.
Jesus explicitly challenged that kind of simplistic reasoning when He spoke about tragic deaths in Luke 13:1–5.
Instead, He used those tragedies to call the living to repentance.
That distinction matters.
Because the point of reading Jezebel's judgment is not to look at someone else's terrible ending and feel spiritually superior.
It is to hear God's warning while we still have breath.
And perhaps that is the part of this story that should trouble us most.
Jezebel's body was consumed after her death.
But her choices had been consuming her life long before that day.
Sin has a way of doing that.
At first, it looks manageable.
One lie.
One secret.
One compromise.
One act of revenge.
One relationship we know is leading us away from God.
One habit we keep defending because surrender would cost us something.
We tell ourselves we can stop whenever we want.
We tell ourselves God understands.
We tell ourselves there will be another opportunity to make things right.
And sometimes there is.
But we are never promised tomorrow.
The danger is not simply that judgment may come unexpectedly.
The danger is that we can become so accustomed to resisting God that we no longer recognize His mercy when it confronts us.
Hebrews 3:15 says:
“To day if ye will hear his voice, harden not your hearts.” (KJV)
Today.
Not when your life becomes convenient.
Not when the secret sin has finally stopped being pleasurable.
Not when the relationship has already collapsed.
Not when the consequences are impossible to hide.
Today.
And now I want you to notice something that changes the direction of this entire story.
There was another person in Scripture whose body was publicly humiliated.
Another person exposed before a watching crowd.
Another person associated with the shame of a brutal death.
But unlike Jezebel, He was not dying under judgment for His own wickedness.
He was completely innocent.
His name is Jesus Christ.
The Son of God was betrayed, condemned, mocked, beaten, and crucified.
Soldiers stripped Him and gambled for His garments.
People insulted Him while He suffered.
His body was wounded.
His blood was shed.
And while Jezebel's story reveals the seriousness of sin and divine judgment, the cross reveals the astonishing mercy of God toward sinners.
Here is the difference we must never forget.
Jezebel's death was part of the judgment announced against her wickedness. Jesus' death was the willing sacrifice of the sinless Savior for the sins of others.
These are not morally equivalent deaths.
But their contrast forces us to confront the two realities we would rather separate.
God is holy.
And God is merciful.
Sin matters.
And grace is real.
The same Bible that records Jezebel's terrible end also declares that God has made a way for sinners to be forgiven.
Isaiah 53:5 says:
“But he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities: the chastisement of our peace was upon him; and with his stripes we are healed.” (KJV)
The Hebrew word פְּשָׁעֵינוּ (pesha'ēnū) means “our transgressions,” referring to our acts of rebellion.
And עֲוֹנֹתֵינוּ ('avonōtēnū) means “our iniquities,” carrying the sense of guilt or wrongdoing.
The prophet was not describing an innocent sufferer who merely inspires us to become better people.
Read in light of the New Testament, the passage points to the suffering Servant whose sacrifice deals with the guilt of sinners.
First Peter 2:24 explicitly applies this truth to Jesus, who bore our sins in His own body on the tree.
And this is where the Gospel becomes personal.
Because Jesus did not go to the cross only for people whose failures look respectable.
He came to save sinners.
People who have lied.
People who have betrayed trust.
People who have manipulated others.
People who have hidden addictions.
People who have ruined relationships.
People who have hurt those they were supposed to protect.
People whose consciences have become exhausted from carrying the weight of their own decisions.
And people who are finally tired of pretending they are innocent.
No sin is made harmless by grace.
No victim's suffering becomes unimportant because a perpetrator asks for forgiveness.
Real repentance does not excuse injustice. It turns away from evil, tells the truth, and seeks to make wrongs right wherever possible.
But no sinner who truly comes to Christ needs to believe that their past is stronger than His power to redeem.
Listen to the invitation in Romans 5:8:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.” (KJV)
While we were still sinners.
Not after we cleaned ourselves up.
Not after we proved we deserved a second chance.
Not after our reputation was restored.
While we were still sinners.
The Greek expression ἔτι ἁμαρτωλῶν ὄντων ἡμῶν (eti hamartōlōn ontōn hēmōn) conveys that very reality: while we were still sinners.
God's love in Christ did not wait for human beings to become worthy of it.
And that is why the Gospel is not merely a warning about how badly sin can end.
It is the announcement that forgiveness and new life are available through the crucified and risen Jesus Christ.
The Greek word μετάνοια (metanoia) means “repentance,” a turning of mind and heart that involves turning away from sin and toward God.
Repentance is not simply feeling frightened by a story like Jezebel's.
It is not crying for five minutes and then returning unchanged to the same deliberate rebellion.
It is coming into the light.
Confessing what is true.
Abandoning the excuses.
And trusting Christ enough to follow Him.
First John 1:9 gives this promise:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” (KJV)
Do you understand how extraordinary that is?
The God who saw Naboth's blood also sees the wrong that has been done to you.
The God who confronted Ahab also sees the sin you have been hiding.
And the God who judges wickedness is the God who gave His Son so that repentant sinners could receive mercy without pretending that evil does not matter.
Maybe you are reading this while carrying a secret nobody knows.
Maybe you have become skilled at smiling in church while feeling spiritually empty.
Maybe you are angry with God because someone else's wickedness shattered your life.
Maybe you are afraid that you have gone too far.
Or perhaps you have been using religion to hide the fact that you have never truly surrendered to Jesus.
I cannot tell you what is inside your heart.
But I can tell you what Scripture says.
Jesus declared in John 6:37:
“Him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out.” (KJV)
That promise is not permission to continue embracing evil.
It is an invitation to come to the Savior.

And if you have been wounded by someone else's cruelty, remember this too: forgiveness does not require you to return to danger, deny what happened, or abandon justice. Christ's mercy is never an excuse for abuse.
The Gospel calls the guilty to repentance and offers hope to the wounded.
That is why we cannot finish Jezebel's story by staring at the ground where her body fell.
We must look toward the empty tomb of Jesus Christ.
Jezebel's story ends with the disgrace of a grave she never received.
Jesus was placed in a tomb, but on the third day He rose again.
Death did not have the final word over Him.
And because He lives, those who belong to Him have the promise of resurrection and eternal life.
This is the heart of our message at Gospel Warrior.
Not because every scandal disappears.
Not because earthly consequences cease to exist.
Not because grace makes sin unimportant.
But because Jesus can redeem sinners, transform lives, restore what can be restored, and give eternal hope to people who could never save themselves.
Maybe your story has chapters you wish had never been written.
Maybe your family knows the damage.
Maybe your children have seen the struggle.
Maybe your marriage carries scars.
Maybe the person you used to be still haunts your memories.
But your past does not have to be the master of your future.
Christ calls you to something more than regret.
He calls you to surrender.
To truth.
To holiness.
To a life made new by grace.
And if something in this article has exposed a place in your heart where you have been resisting God, do not rush past it.
Pray.
Confess.
Seek help where help is needed.
Make restitution where possible.
Open your Bible.
Return to fellowship with faithful believers.
And come to Jesus.
You do not need a dramatic public confession in a comment section to prove your repentance. God sees the heart.
You may never know how much hope another struggling believer receives from seeing that they are not alone.
And if this message reminded you of someone who has been drifting away from God, consider sharing it with them personally.
Not to shame them.
Not to accuse them of being Jezebel.
But to remind them that repentance is urgent and the mercy of Jesus is real.
Invite your family, your friends, believers who feel spiritually exhausted, Christians who have grown complacent, and even people who are still searching for the truth about Jesus.
Because the purpose of this ministry is not simply to collect reactions beneath a powerful story.
It is to help people encounter the Word of God, understand the Gospel, and grow in faithful obedience to Christ.
And there is another way you can help this mission continue.
But voluntary financial support can be one meaningful expression of Christian generosity.
Second Corinthians 9:7 reminds us that giving should be done willingly, not reluctantly or under compulsion, because God loves a cheerful giver.
Those items can serve as reminders of Scripture, encouragement in daily life, or meaningful gifts for others.
It is the opportunity to participate in helping more people hear the truth about Jesus.
Both forms of support are appreciated.
Because the greatest goal of Gospel Warrior is not that you become attached to a page.
It is that you become more deeply rooted in Jesus Christ.
Before you leave, return with me one final time to that palace window.
Picture the queen looking down at the approaching judgment.
Remember the power she once held.
Remember the innocent people who suffered.
Remember the warnings that had been spoken.
And remember what the men found when they returned.
A skull.
Feet.
The palms of her hands.
Everything that once made Jezebel appear untouchable had failed her.
But the final question of this article is not whether you are as wicked as Jezebel.
It is whether you are willing to listen when God calls you to repentance.
You are still breathing.
You are still able to hear His Word.
And the Gospel is still being proclaimed.
Do not confuse God's patience with His approval of sin.
Second Peter 3:9 teaches that the Lord is patient, not willing that any should perish, but that all should come to repentance.
That patience is not something to exploit.
It is mercy to receive.
If you have been running from Christ, turn to Him.
If you have been hiding your sin, bring it into His light.
If you have been wounded by evil, entrust your pain to the Savior who sees and cares.
If you have fallen, do not make your failure your final identity.
And if you already belong to Jesus, live today with humility, gratitude, and faithfulness.
Because one day, every earthly title will fall silent.
Every human reputation will lose its power.
Every possession will be left behind.
But the promise of eternal life in the risen Christ will remain.
Jezebel's crown could not save her from judgment. Your past cannot save you either—but Jesus Christ can save everyone who comes to Him in repentant faith.
